Patient note:
A 44-year-old man checked in to the same-day procedure unit this morning for an outpatient arthroscopic debridement of a chronic left ankle impingement that the orthopedic surgeon anticipates will last roughly forty minutes under monitored anesthesia care with a planned discharge home later today. He reports that the ankle has limited his weekend trail running mileage over the past six months, but he continues to bicycle to work and climb three flights of stairs to his office each day without shortness of breath, chest discomfort, or need for assistance, demonstrating his usual unrestricted ambulation. The patient has not been admitted to a hospital, undergone another operation, received intravenous antibiotics, or worn any splints, casts, or braces in the past thirty days. He denies recent fevers, rigors, unexplained hypotension, or systemic infections and recalls no episodes of heart failure, strokes, fractures, spinal cord injury, major trauma, or myocardial infarction. Past medical history is notable for cosmetically bothersome, tortuous blue veins that began along the great-saphenous territory of both calves in his mid-thirties when he worked long retail shifts, and over the past month he has noticed that the lower legs feel heavy and appear puffier by evening, prompting him to purchase knee-high compression stockings that reduce the tightness by morning. Duplex imaging obtained at an outside vascular clinic one year ago confirmed superficial venous reflux without thrombus, and no clinician has ever diagnosed him with a clot in the legs or lungs. During a life-insurance physical two years ago, fasting bloodwork revealed total homocysteine persistently in the mid-teens micromoles per liter despite normal vitamin B₁₂ and folate levels; genetic testing at that time was negative for common prothrombotic mutations, specifically including Factor V Leiden, and antiphospholipid screening showed normal anticardiolipin antibody titers. He now takes an over-the-counter B-complex tablet daily. He has no personal or first-degree family history of deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, miscarriages, cancers, inflammatory bowel disease, or connective-tissue disorders. He denies chronic cough, sputum production, wheeze, or steroid use and quit social cigarette smoking more than a decade ago after a five-pack-year exposure. Current medications include only the vitamin supplement and occasional ibuprofen, which he stopped three days ago following pre-operative instructions; he does not take hormones, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, glucocorticoids, or antiplatelet drugs. Socially, he drinks two glasses of red wine on weekends, denies illicit drug use, and maintains a body-mass index of 26 kg m⁻² through regular exercise and a pescatarian diet. Vital signs fifteen minutes prior to anesthesia assessment show temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, heart rate 74 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respiratory rate 16 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. He is alert, oriented, and seated comfortably on the stretcher. Inspection of both lower extremities reveals serpiginous dilated superficial veins coursing up the medial calves with mild, bilateral, non-tender pitting edema that indents to 1 cm above the malleoli and resolves after overnight elevation; calf circumferences are 39 cm on the right and 40 cm on the left, and there is no localized warmth, erythema, or palpable cord. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2 + and symmetric. Cardiovascular examination demonstrates brisk carotid upstrokes, a regular rate and rhythm, and crisp S₁/S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pulsation is not elevated. Lungs are clear to auscultation with good air entry bilaterally. The abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds. Neurologic screening confirms intact cranial nerves, full strength, and normal sensation; there is no focal deficit. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class II, adequate thyromental distance, and full cervical extension suggestive of straightforward mask ventilation and intubation if needed. A single 20-gauge peripheral IV placed in the right forearm this morning is running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; he has never had a tunneled catheter, implantable port, or peripherally inserted central line. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn at 0600 demonstrate hemoglobin 15.0 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 44 %, platelet count 240 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.96 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 22 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A resting twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-segment changes, and a portable anterior–posterior chest radiograph taken for ankle immobilization hardware screening reveals clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided one hour ago, and pneumatic calf compressors are at the foot of the bed awaiting activation once anesthesia begins; no anticoagulant has yet been administered while the team finalizes the plan for nerve-block analgesia and same-day discharge instructions.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums perioperative venous thromboembolism risk factors. The applicable criteria are:
- Age 41–60 years: age 44 → 1.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 26 → 1.
- Visible varicose veins: dilated, tortuous superficial calf veins → 1.
- Current swollen legs: bilateral pitting ankle edema on examination → 1, distinct from the varicose veins.
- Minor surgery lasting <45 minutes: planned 40-minute outpatient arthroscopy → 1.
- Elevated homocysteine: persistent elevation on prior testing → 3.
No additional factors are documented: he is ambulatory, has no personal or family history of VTE, and has a peripheral IV rather than a central line.
Total: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8.
Final answer: 8
